hero.headline: Fourth of July weekend brings elevated crash risk as impaired driving deaths spike 44 percent
hero.teaser: Last Fourth of July, 579 people died in car crashes nationwide with nearly 4 in 10 deaths involving impaired driving. Local residents say they plan to use rideshares and designated drivers for holiday celebrations.
hero.body:
Independence Day stands out as one of the most hazardous holidays on American roads, though advance preparation can make a critical difference in safety outcomes. Last Fourth of July, 579 people lost their lives in vehicle crashes across the nation. The concerning part is that nearly 4 in 10 of those deaths involved impaired driving, a rate substantially higher than the typical 30% seen during the rest of the year. Research shows that deadly crashes increase by 44% specifically on Independence Day compared to other days.

Federal statistics reveal that teenagers account for about 10% of these holiday fatalities. The spike in dangerous driving during this period has prompted increased awareness campaigns focused on prevention. Rideshare services like Uber and Lyft have reported surge demand as people increasingly turn to these apps to serve as their designated drivers. Safety advocates recommend that celebrants plan ahead by using rideshares, taxis, or public transportation rather than driving themselves after consuming alcohol or becoming fatigued from holiday activities.

Residents in downtown West Palm Beach demonstrate they are taking these safety messages to heart. Scott explained his Independence Day plans involve paddle boarding but noted he will arrange for a designated driver to transport his group to and from the location. Pamela shared that she plans to use Uber for her holiday celebration travel. Carlos captured the sentiment simply by saying, "Definitely want to have a fun time and make it home in one piece."

For those planning to use rideshare services during the busy holiday weekend, several money-saving strategies can help reduce costs during peak demand periods. Timing matters significantly, so leaving early or waiting until surge pricing subsides can result in lower fares. Walking a few blocks away from congested areas makes pickups easier and may reduce wait times. Additionally, comparing prices across different rideshare platforms before booking allows users to find the best available rates. By combining smart planning with these practical tips, holiday celebrants can enjoy Independence Day while prioritizing safety for themselves and others on the road.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Zoning Commission recommends denial of data center near Arden community
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Zoning Commission on Thursday recommended against building a controversial data center near the Arden community after months of pushback f.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Zoning Commission on Thursday recommended against building a controversial data center near the Arden community after months of pushback from residents in the western communities. More than 100 people packed a public hearing held at the Vista Center located off Jog Road regarding the data center proposal known as "Project Tango." The commission recommended that county commissioners deny the project based on a lack of understanding of the new technology and whether the project would be heavy or light industrial.

Thursday's recommendation comes after Palm Beach County planning staff earlier this week recommended that county commissioners approve the project. The proposed data center site sits approximately 1,100 feet from the Arden community and the recently opened Saddleview Elementary School. Area residents have cited several concerns regarding the project, including potential environmental impacts. Palm Beach County commissioners will consider the zoning commission's decision when they hold a July 15 meeting on the project.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach teenager Harper Aberman to represent Team USA at Sailing World Championship in France
cards.body:
A Jensen Beach teenager will represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France this weekend, following a sailing journey that started at a Pennsylvania summer camp when she was four years old. Harper Aberman's grandparents enrolled her in a four-week sailing program, where she discovered her passion for the sport. "They then decided to throw my cousin and me into summer camp, where they then did a four-week course, and my cousin hated it, and I fell in love with it, and I ended up going for eight weeks," Aberman said. After her family relocated to Jensen Beach, she joined the green fleet program at the US Sailing Center of Martin County, where her competitive sailing career began to develop.

Aberman identifies as an adrenaline junkie and is drawn to the sport's most challenging conditions. She acknowledges her struggles with windy weather, saying "When it's windy, I've always struggled to stay upright and stay out of the water." Despite downplaying her own abilities, Aberman has compiled an impressive record of competitive achievements. She has won numerous tournaments, placed in several national competitions, and has earned recognition as one of the most prominent names in youth sailing. "That is where the sailing adventure took off for me," she said of the US Sailing Center of Martin County.

The selection to compete for Team USA arrived during Spring Break with an email that sparked celebration in the Aberman household. "It was during Spring Break, I got the email. I started screaming, my parents started screaming, and we were like, 'This is not real. We're going to Europe this summer,'" Aberman said. She has spent recent weeks preparing for the international competition through training in Spain before heading to the French venue. Racing is scheduled to begin Monday.

Aberman's preparation has been rigorous as she approaches the championship. "We plan on taking the waters Monday for racing, and it's just been a lot of recovery and a lot of time and effort out on the water, but it's definitely going to be worth it. Especially in the venue we're in," she said. The combination of intensive training and recovery time has shaped her readiness for competing on the world stage.

cards.headline: Orlando woman killed by alligator in Econlockhatchee River as FWC investigates third attack in seven days
cards.teaser: Brittany Clark, a 31-year-old Orlando woman, died Sunday after an alligator attacked her while she was swimming in the Econlockhatchee River at Little Big Econ .
cards.body:
Brittany Clark, a 31-year-old Orlando woman, died Sunday after an alligator attacked her while swimming in Econlockhatchee River at Little Big Econ State Forest in Central Florida. Her boyfriend, who was present during the attack, said Clark loved going out on the water every chance she could and never imagined this nightmare would happen. An online fundraiser described the incident as a "completely bizarre accident" that took the life of an avid bike rider and dog lover.

Following the attack, Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officials captured and killed two alligators. The first was a 13-foot reptile found near where Clark was badly bitten, and the second was a 12-and-a-half-foot alligator about a half mile away. A 911 call from one of Clark's friends described the bite as "horrible." The FWC has submitted DNA samples from both alligators to a lab in Gainesville for testing to determine if they were involved in the deadly attack. Officials will examine the animals' mouths and stomachs. Frank Robb, who has more than three decades of experience dealing with Florida alligators, noted that eyewitness accounts from people present during the attack will help the investigation. This incident marks the third gator attack within seven days reported in Central Florida.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Marine Unit rescues two boaters after vessel sinks in Intracoastal Waterway
cards.teaser: Two boaters are safe after their vessel sank in the Intracoastal Waterway on Wednesday, thanks to a quick response from marine deputies and the life-saving deci.
cards.body:
Two boaters are safe after their vessel sank in the Intracoastal Waterway on July 1, thanks to a quick response from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Marine Unit and the life-saving decision to wear life jackets. Deputies responded to reports of a small motorized boat taking on water and becoming submerged. Both occupants ended up in the water when their boat went down, but they were wearing life jackets that kept them afloat while help arrived. Body-worn camera footage captured the rescue as it unfolded.

"This incident serves as an important reminder that wearing a life jacket can save your life," the sheriff's office said in a Facebook post. "We're grateful this call ended safely and proud of the swift response by our Marine Unit deputies who are always ready to answer the call."

hero.headline: Lantana veteran gets roof lien removed after months of frustration with Boynton Beach contractor
hero.teaser: Stephen McCoy, a disabled and retired veteran, had a nearly $7,000 lien removed from his Lantana home after a contractor failed to pay suppliers.
hero.body:
Stephen McCoy, a disabled and retired veteran, hired Seabreeze Roofing and Sheet Metal in Boynton Beach to replace his aging roof before hurricane season. He made six payments to the company totaling more than $17,000 and said the work was mostly satisfactory. However, two holes remained unfinished on the back of his home, and when McCoy tried to get them fixed, the contractor stopped responding to his calls, texts and emails. Screenshots showed he had attempted to reach the company multiple times starting in January, including a follow-up email from a worker on February 5 who promised the owner would call. That call never came.

The situation worsened when McCoy received letters from Gulfeagle Supply, a material supplier, warning that a nearly $7,000 lien had been filed against his home. According to the lien document, Gulfeagle Supply had provided materials to Seabreeze Roofing for McCoy's property but had not been paid. McCoy found himself caught in the middle of a payment dispute between the contractor and the supplier. "They're basically saying they never paid them the $6,900, so now they took a lien out on my house," McCoy said. The prospect of dealing with attorneys or court proceedings added to his anxiety and financial burden.

After months without resolution, McCoy turned to WPTV for help. Investigative reporter Kate Hussey visited Seabreeze Roofing and spoke directly with the owner about the unpaid materials and the lien on McCoy's home. Although the owner declined to comment on camera, citing legal reasons, the conversation prompted immediate action. Within an hour, Hussey returned to McCoy's home with a final waiver of lien, signed by Gulfeagle Supply and notarized, officially removing the lien from his property. McCoy was stunned by the swift resolution. "Oh my God, how did you do that? Are you serious?" he asked.

The breakthrough also led to a commitment from the contractor to complete the unfinished work. About an hour after receiving the lien waiver, McCoy sent WPTV a photo showing crews back on his roof finishing the job. McCoy expressed his relief and gratitude, saying the lien and incomplete repairs had caused him immense stress. "I've been going through hell," he said. "You just don't know how much of a burden this was off of me." After months of frustration and unanswered messages, the intervention finally provided McCoy with the resolution he had been seeking.

hero.headline: Florida manufactured home owners can now apply for storm-hardening and repair funding starting in August
hero.teaser: Manufactured home owners in Martin, St. Lucie, Indian River and Okeechobee counties can access $167 million in state funding for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits under a new law that took effect Wednesday.
hero.body:
Senate Bill 594 took effect on July 1st, making $167 million in state affordable housing funding available to mobile and manufactured home owners seeking emergency repairs and storm-hardening improvements. The law represents a significant shift in how Florida addresses the vulnerability of older manufactured homes that cannot withstand modern storms. The change comes after an investigation revealed that nearly 700,000 of Florida's more than 1 million mobile and manufactured homes were built before current federal safety standards, leaving them at risk during severe weather events.

The push for this funding stems from an EF-3 tornado that destroyed 138 homes in the Spanish Lakes Country Club Community of Fort Pierce, killing six residents. Following that disaster, state lawmakers expanded access to SHIP funding, which traditionally supported affordable housing programs. Now, eligible manufactured homeowners can use these funds for lot rent, rehabilitation, emergency repairs, and storm-hardening retrofits. Many residents living in these homes are seniors on fixed incomes who cannot afford the substantial costs of upgrades, which often range from $10,000 to $15,000 per home.

Martin County Human Services will launch an online portal in August where residents can submit applications. Applicants can either complete the application online or request a paper version by calling the county office. Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services emphasizes that funding operates on a first-come, first-served basis, making it crucial for homeowners to gather necessary paperwork quickly. About 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically between $1 million and $1.5 million, can now be directed toward manufactured home assistance.

The application timeline varies across counties. Okeechobee County is updating its local housing assistance plan to comply with the new law and plans to offer programs once funding becomes available. St. Lucie County is awaiting final state guidance before announcing its specific application process. Indian River County will present the legislative changes to its Board on August 18th, with a September 30th deadline to submit its plan to the state. Residents can prepare now by visiting the Florida Housing Finance Corporation website, selecting their county or city, and checking income eligibility requirements and available funding amounts. Stellatos notes that while individual counties follow different timelines, they generally operate on a calendar established by the Florida Housing Coalition.

cards.headline: Volunteers in Medicine clinic in Martin County sees more patients after ACA subsidies expired, has room for hundreds more
cards.teaser: The free medical clinic in Martin County has seen about 20 new patients after enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies expired, but estimates show there could be upwards of 500 people in the county who lost access to health insurance.
cards.body:
Volunteers in Medicine, a free clinic serving low-income families in Martin County, is seeing increased patient demand after enhanced subsidies through the Affordable Care Act expired at the start of 2024. The expiration of the financial assistance program has left many people without health insurance and, in some cases, without access to medical care. Dr. Jordan Bromberg, medical director of Volunteers in Medicine, said more than 200,000 people in Florida did not renew their health insurance through the ACA this year. While only about 20 patients have turned to the clinic after losing ACA coverage, estimates show there could be upwards of 500 people in Martin County who lost access. "We have the capacity for more," Bromberg said.

Rokaya McGarry is among those who sought care at the clinic after losing her health insurance. She said panic set in after the enhanced subsidies expired, as she could no longer afford coverage. McGarry fell ill after losing her mother and called the clinic in desperation. Within a day, Volunteers in Medicine took over her care. To qualify for services, individuals must earn under $39,990 per year, or under $82,500 for a family of four. The clinic provides free medical care with no strings attached.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz immigration detention facility closed after one year of controversy and questions about $1 billion cost
cards.teaser: The controversial Everglades immigration detention facility opened by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and President Donald Trump on July 1, 2025 closed in June after detaining roughly 21,000 people, leaving questions about who will pay the estimated $1 billion cost.
cards.body:
One year after opening on July 1, 2025, Florida's Alligator Alcatraz immigration detention facility has closed after becoming one of the most controversial detention camps in the country. President Donald Trump announced the opening alongside Gov. Ron DeSantis, describing it as a place to house what he called the most dangerous migrants. The state used emergency powers to commandeer an old landing strip belonging to Miami-Dade County and built the facility in eight days using emergency funding and no-bid contracts through the Florida Division of Emergency Management. Trump said FEMA would pay for the facility. Using ICE's own data, investigations uncovered that about 70 percent of detainees had no criminal record, contradicting government claims that only criminals would be housed there.

The facility faced multiple federal lawsuits challenging its operations and legality. The American Civil Liberties Union sued over detainees' access to legal counsel, citing restrictions on attorney visits and monitored phone calls. Friends of the Everglades, led by Director Eve Samples, joined the Miccosukee Tribe and other environmental groups in a separate lawsuit claiming construction violated the National Environmental Policy Act. On June 16, ICE confirmed all detainees had been removed in preparation for hurricane season. DeSantis said 21,000 detainees were deported through the facility. A stalled $608 million FEMA grant left Florida taxpayers covering costs estimated at more than $1 billion. Both lawsuits remain active.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman raises funds for best friend's family after Venezuela earthquakes
cards.teaser: Carla Alvarado of West Palm Beach launched a GoFundMe campaign to support her best friend's family after two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira last week.
cards.body:
Alessandra De La Correa spent six agonizing hours wondering whether her parents were alive after two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira last week, collapsing buildings and killing several family members. Her best friend since high school, Carla Alvarado, who now lives in West Palm Beach, woke De La Correa with nonstop phone calls in the middle of the night after the earthquake struck. De La Correa lost her 17-year-old cousin Claudia, her grandmother, her uncle and his wife. Claudia, a volleyball player who had planned to study dentistry, had been rehearsing a dance routine with classmates when the building collapsed. De La Correa's uncle, a former Navy member, searched through the rubble in darkness and found Claudia dead beneath the debris. He stayed behind to help rescue her trapped best friend, who was asking not to be left to die, but the girl was later killed after another section of the structure collapsed during rescue efforts.

The earthquakes also destroyed De La Correa's parents' home and businesses. Her mother's children's clothing store had been located inside a shopping mall that collapsed entirely. Her parents survived only because they had closed the store early and were driving home when the earthquake struck. Feeling powerless from abroad, Alvarado launched a GoFundMe campaign aiming to raise $15,000 to support De La Correa's relatives. De La Correa said the support from friends and strangers has become a lifeline as her parents return daily to the ruins of their apartment building searching for salvageable belongings.

cards.headline: Lantana veteran gets lien removed and roof fixed after contractor dispute
cards.teaser: Stephen McCoy, a disabled and retired veteran in Lantana, had a nearly $7,000 lien removed from his home and unfinished roof repairs completed after a local news station intervened.
cards.body:
Stephen McCoy, a disabled and retired veteran in Lantana, hired Seabreeze Roofing and Sheet Metal in Boynton Beach to replace his nearly 20-year-old roof ahead of hurricane season. He made six payments totaling more than $17,000 but said the company left two holes unfinished on the back side of his home. When McCoy tried to follow up starting Jan. 10, he called, texted and emailed the company multiple times. A worker responded on Feb. 5 saying the owner would call, but McCoy said he never heard from the owner again. Letters from Gulfeagle Supply began arriving warning that the company had filed a nearly $7,000 lien with the county on his home because Seabreeze Roofing had not paid for materials used on the project.

WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey contacted Seabreeze Roofing's owner, who declined to comment on camera citing legal reasons. Within an hour, Hussey returned to McCoy's home with a final waiver of lien signed by Gulfeagle Supply and notarized, lifting the lien. About an hour after receiving the waiver, McCoy sent WPTV a photo showing crews back on his roof finishing the unfinished work. McCoy said he felt relieved after months of frustration and worry about potentially having to hire an attorney.

hero.headline: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach offers sea turtle nesting programs through September
hero.teaser: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach is offering educational and interactive programs during peak sea turtle nesting season this summer.
hero.body:
The center said guests can participate in seasonal experiences through September, including guided Turtle Walks, the Hatchling Discovery Program, Hatchling Releases, Tidal Tots and Plastic Free July Community Action Day. According to Loggerhead Marinelife Center, the programs are designed to give visitors an opportunity to learn more about sea turtle conservation along one of the world's busiest sea turtle nesting beaches.

The center's Turtle Walk program allows participants to observe the nesting process while learning about sea turtle biology, conservation and ongoing research efforts. Educational demonstrations during the programs may include the use of red-light headlamps, amber lighting, night scopes and research tag scanning equipment. Loggerhead Marinelife Center also said its education and research departments work together during nesting season to collect and analyze data related to nesting activity and hatchling success.

Sea turtle nesting season in Florida typically runs from March through October. Conservation groups continue encouraging beachgoers to turn off beachfront lighting at night, properly dispose of trash and avoid disturbing nesting turtles or hatchlings. Registration information and program details are available through Loggerhead Marinelife Center.

cards.headline: North Palm Beach hosts Fourth of July fireworks, pool party and America 250 celebration Friday
cards.body:
North Palm Beach will celebrate Independence Day on July 4 with a full day of family-friendly activities, live entertainment and fireworks at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse. Organizers say this year's event also recognizes America's 250th anniversary, bringing added significance to the annual holiday tradition in Palm Beach County.

The free community event begins with a pool party at 11 a.m. at the country club pool area. Guests can enjoy a water slide, DJ entertainment, games, activities, food, beverages and a poolside satellite bar. Beginning at 4:30 p.m., families can participate in cornhole, Connect 4, giant Jenga and face painting. Live music from Solstice Reign is expected to begin around 6 p.m. The Clubhouse will also open at 4:30 p.m. to serve a Fourth of July barbecue buffet. Ashley Shipman, director of parks and recreation, said the golf course will offer one of the best locations to watch the fireworks display, which is scheduled for 9 p.m.

hero.headline: Florida Attorney General Ashley Moody marks first anniversary of Working Families Tax Cut benefitting state residents
hero.teaser: Florida Attorney General Ashley Moody is touting the one-year anniversary of the Working Families Tax Cut Act, which eliminated federal taxes on Social Security, tips for service workers, and overtime pay.
hero.body:
Ashley Moody is celebrating the one-year milestone of what she describes as the largest tax cut in American history. President Donald Trump signed the Working Families Tax Cut Act into law on July 4, 2024, and Moody has been a vocal supporter of the legislation. As the first anniversary approaches, she is drawing attention to the tangible financial benefits that have reached Floridians and Americans across the country.

The measure eliminated federal taxes on three major categories of income: Social Security benefits, tips earned by service workers, and overtime pay. Moody has made clear her commitment to this tax relief approach. "It's not the government's money. It's your money, and you should be allowed to keep as much of it as possible. That is why I supported no tax on Social Security, no tax on tips, and no tax on overtime," she said in a statement released Thursday. She emphasized her intention to continue pursuing tax cuts and fiscal responsibility in her future role. "In the year since the tax cuts became law, it is clear that we delivered for real relief for Floridians, and as your U.S. Senator, I will continue to look for ways to cut taxes, eliminate waste and support economic growth here in the Sunshine State."

The numbers released by Moody's office demonstrate the widespread impact of the legislation. Nationally, Americans have claimed $82 billion in individual relief, with 97 percent of taxpayers experiencing a reduction in federal taxes during the most recent filing season. Specifically, 7.5 million Americans paid no federal tax on tips, 29 million avoided taxes on overtime earnings, and 35 million seniors claimed a larger tax deduction. Florida residents have fared particularly well under the law, receiving the largest average federal tax refunds in the nation. The average refund for Florida filers reached approximately $4,500, significantly exceeding the national average of $3,300.

The legislation also created new financial opportunities for younger Americans and their families. More than 5.5 million child-owned investment accounts have been opened since the law took effect, with 1.4 million of those accounts currently eligible for a $1,000 Treasury contribution. Parents of babies born between 2025 and 2028 can take advantage of this benefit if they choose to participate in the program. These provisions represent an effort to build long-term financial security for the next generation of Americans.

cards.headline: Orlando woman killed by alligator in Econlockhatchee River as FWC investigates third attack in seven days
cards.teaser: Brittany Clark, a 31-year-old Orlando woman, died Sunday after an alligator attacked her while she was swimming in the Econlockhatchee River at Little Big Econ .
cards.body:
Brittany Clark, a 31-year-old Orlando woman, died Sunday after an alligator attacked her while swimming in Econlockhatchee River at Little Big Econ State Forest in Central Florida. Her boyfriend, who was present during the attack, said Clark loved going out on the water every chance she could and never imagined this nightmare would happen. An online fundraiser described the incident as a "completely bizarre accident" that took the life of an avid bike rider and dog lover.

Following the attack, Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officials captured and killed two alligators. The first was a 13-foot reptile found near where Clark was badly bitten, and the second was a 12-and-a-half-foot alligator about a half mile away. A 911 call from one of Clark's friends described the bite as "horrible." The FWC has submitted DNA samples from both alligators to a lab in Gainesville for testing to determine if they were involved in the deadly attack. Officials will examine the animals' mouths and stomachs. Frank Robb, who has more than three decades of experience dealing with Florida alligators, noted that eyewitness accounts from people present during the attack will help the investigation. This incident marks the third gator attack within seven days reported in Central Florida.

cards.headline: St. Petersburg City Council Member Brandi Gabbard challenges Mayor Ken Welch over Tropicana Field redevelopment selection
cards.teaser: St. Petersburg City Council Member Brandi Gabbard is urging the city to pause before moving forward with Mayor Ken Welch's pick of The Burg Bid for the massive Tropicana Field redevelopment, citing concerns that city staff found no clear front-runner.
cards.body:
St. Petersburg City Council Member Brandi Gabbard is calling for the city to pause before moving forward with Mayor Ken Welch's selection of The Burg Bid for the Tropicana Field redevelopment. Gabbard points out that city staff, after reviewing final proposals, found no clear front-runner, raising questions about the pace of the decision. In a statement Thursday, her campaign highlighted that staff stopped short of naming a clear favorite, suggesting the decision deserves more scrutiny. "When our own internal experts review these multi-billion-dollar proposals and state that no clear favorite emerges, it is a definitive sign that we need to slow down," Gabbard said. She previously won support for her push to slow the process and allow for an independent review by the Urban Land Institute Tampa Bay.

Welch announced Thursday that he intends to move forward with The Burg Bid, led by Blake Investment Partners and developer Thompson Whitney Blake. The proposal includes an estimated $8 billion redevelopment plan and about 3,600 affordable and workforce housing units, along with office, retail, hotel, entertainment and open space components. Gabbard argues that Welch's focus on Tropicana Field redevelopment over the past five years has come at a cost to basic city services and long-term planning, with city staff spending two years almost exclusively on negotiations. She contends that resiliency planning and permitting reforms were sidelined. Any deal must still go before City Council, where Gabbard says she will push for transparency, fiscal responsibility, and stronger assurances that residents stay at the center of the redevelopment.

cards.headline: Democratic first responder Bernard Taylor raises $563,000 in second quarter for Florida's 21st Congressional District race
cards.teaser: Bernard Taylor, a Democratic EMT and paramedic, announced his campaign raised just under $563,000 in the second quarter with more than 25,000 individual donations averaging $22 apiece for his race to unseat Republican U.S. Rep. Brian Mast.
cards.body:
Democratic first responder Bernard Taylor raised just under $563,000 in the second quarter of 2025 for his bid to unseat Republican U.S. Rep. Brian Mast in Florida's 21st Congressional District. Taylor, an EMT/paramedic, received more than 25,000 individual donations averaging $22 apiece. His campaign declined all corporate PAC money and special-interest donations, with more than 93 percent of contributions from April 1 to June 30 coming through mobile devices and roughly 41 percent routed through digital fundraising platform ActBlue. "I'm humbled by the incredible support we've received from thousands of people who believe it's time for new leadership in Washington," Taylor said. "These contributions are coming from working families, retirees, veterans, teachers, first responders, and neighbors who want a representative who understands their challenges and will fight for them every day."

A fourth-generation Floridian, Taylor prioritizes affordable healthcare access, educational investment, job creation, housing affordability, environmental protection and representing constituents over political insiders. He believes his emergency medical services experience has exposed him to rising healthcare costs and limited options facing families across the coastal district stretching from Royal Palm heel in Palm Beach County north through Martin and St. Lucie counties. About 57.5 percent of district voters, whose boundaries changed under a congressional map Gov. Ron DeSantis and the GOP-dominated Legislature approved in April, voted for President Donald Trump in 2024. Taylor faces Primary opponent U.S. Coast Guard veteran James Martin, who entered the second quarter with nearly $307,000 raised. The primary is scheduled for August 18, followed by the general election on November 3.

cards.headline: Senate candidate Alex Vindman raises $8.5 million in second quarter for race against Ashley Moody
cards.teaser: Democratic Senate candidate Alex Vindman reported raising $8.5 million over the past three months, bringing his total fundraising to about $16.7 million as he challenges Republican incumbent Ashley Moody in what is shaping up to be one of the most closely watched Senate contests of the cycle.
cards.body:
Democratic Senate candidate Alex Vindman raised $8.5 million in the second quarter, bringing his total fundraising to approximately $16.7 million as he challenges Republican incumbent Ashley Moody. According to his campaign, more than 114,000 donors have contributed, with an average donation under $35. Vindman's campaign characterizes this as grassroots support, noting it has not accepted corporate PAC money and is not beholden to special interests. Vindman said his campaign demonstrates people are seeking a change candidate who will fight to lower costs including homeowners insurance, fuel and groceries.

Vindman's second quarter fundraising exceeded his first quarter total of $8 million, which significantly outpaced Moody's first quarter haul of $2.6 million. However, at the end of the first quarter, Moody maintained a slight fundraising edge with $8.4 million compared to Vindman's just under $8.2 million. Moody's second quarter numbers have not yet been released. Vindman said Florida voters are frustrated by rising gas, grocery and insurance costs and are ready for change. He stated his campaign has momentum and is earning support across the political spectrum, including from Democrats, independents and Republicans.

cards.headline: Former Florida Democratic Party Chair Allison Tant endorses Charlie Crist for St. Petersburg Mayor
cards.teaser: Allison Tant is supporting Charlie Crist's campaign for St. Petersburg Mayor based on a decadeslong political relationship with the former Governor as he looks to return to public office.
cards.body:
Allison Tant, former Chair of the Florida Democratic Party, is endorsing Charlie Crist's campaign for St. Petersburg Mayor based on a decades-long political relationship. Tant has known Crist through his service as state Senator, Governor and Congressman. "I'm delighted to see him take this chance to return to public service. He shows up, he listens, he rolls up his sleeves and takes action to address the work of caring for others and his community," Tant said. "He will be an excellent Mayor and I wholeheartedly endorse his campaign for Mayor of St. Petersburg."

Crist announced the endorsement Thursday, praising Tant for her longtime advocacy for students, families and Floridians with disabilities and her service as former Chair of the Florida Democratic Party. "Allison has spent her career fighting for the people who need a voice most, from students and families to Floridians with disabilities. As a former Chair of the Florida Democratic Party and a respected leader in Tallahassee, she knows what real public service looks like," Crist said. The endorsement comes days after Crist announced a larger slate of Democratic leaders backing his campaign against incumbent Mayor Ken Welch. The nonpartisan St. Petersburg Mayor's race has drawn significant attention from Democratic elected officials and activists, with City Council Member Brandi Gabbard also polling with double digit support.

cards.headline: Nevada Congressman Steven Horsford backs Kendrick Meek Jr. in Florida's 24th Congressional District race, joins TPS effort
cards.teaser: Steven Horsford of Nevada, Chair Emeritus of the Congressional Black Caucus, is endorsing Democrat Kendrick Meek Jr. for Florida's 24th Congressional District and joining him Thursday to discuss efforts to extend temporary protected status following the Supreme Court's recent decision.
cards.body:
Steven Horsford of Nevada, Chair Emeritus of the Congressional Black Caucus, is endorsing Kendrick Meek Jr. for Florida's 24th Congressional District. Horsford will join Meek in the district Thursday at Piman Bouk Restaurant in Miami for a roundtable with local Haitian leaders and community advocates at 12:30 p.m., with a press availability at 1:30 p.m. The visit follows the Supreme Court's decision last week allowing President Donald Trump to end temporary protected status designation. Horsford, who serves on the Ways and Means Committee and represents Nevada's 4th Congressional District, praised Meek's family history of public service. "Whether defending fundamental rights or creating pathways to true economic mobility, Kendrick does not back down from tough fights," Horsford said. "He has the experience, the heartbeat of his community, and a track record of action that South Florida needs right now."

Meek, a University of Miami-trained lawyer, is one of seven Democrats running in CD 24, which covers Miami Gardens in Miami-Dade and Hollywood, Miramar, and Pembroke Park in Broward County. His background includes work as a House Judiciary Committee intern, a legal assistant with the Human Rights Campaign, and service at the federal Office of Management and Budget. He now practices land use, zoning, and real estate development law at LSN Law. Other Democratic candidates include Miami-Dade Commissioner Oliver Gilbert, state Sen. Shevrin Jones, physician-veteran Rudy Moise and former County Commissioner Jean Monestime. More than 68.7 percent of voters in the district backed Kamala Harris in 2024. The Democratic Primary is scheduled for August 18, followed by the General Election on November 3.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County marine deputies rescue two after boat sinks in Intracoastal Waterway
cards.teaser: Two boaters were pulled from the water Wednesday after their vessel sank in the Intracoastal Waterway. Both were wearing life jackets.
cards.body:
Two boaters are safe after their vessel sank in the Intracoastal Waterway on Wednesday, thanks to a quick response from St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Marine Unit deputies and their decision to wear life jackets. The Marine Unit responded to reports of a small motorized boat taking on water and becoming submerged on July 1. Body-worn camera footage captured the rescue as it unfolded.

Both occupants ended up in the water when their boat went down, but deputies said they were wearing life jackets that kept them afloat while help arrived. Marine Unit deputies quickly located the pair in the water and safely brought them aboard their patrol vessel. The boaters were then transported back to the boat ramp without any injuries reported. The sheriff's office said the incident serves as an important reminder that wearing a life jacket can save your life and expressed gratitude that the call ended safely, praising the swift response by Marine Unit deputies.

cards.headline: Deadly crashes spike on Fourth of July weekend, rideshares see surge demand
cards.teaser: Last Fourth of July, 579 people died in car crashes nationwide, with nearly 40% involving impaired driving. Rideshare apps are experiencing surge demand as celebrants plan safe rides home.
cards.body:
The Fourth of July ranks as one of America's most dangerous holidays for drivers. Last Fourth of July, 579 people died in car crashes nationwide. Nearly 4 in 10 of those deaths involved impaired driving, significantly higher than the typical 30% rate seen throughout the year. Historical data shows deadly crashes spike by 44% on Independence Day. Teenagers make up about 10% of these holiday fatalities, according to federal statistics.

Rideshare apps like Uber and Lyft are experiencing surge demand as celebrants use them as designated drivers. Local safety campaigns encourage everyone to plan ahead using rideshares, taxis, or public transportation. Local residents in downtown West Palm Beach say they are making smart choices. Scott said he will have a designated truck driver drop him off and pick him up. Pamela said she will take an Uber to celebrate. To save money on rides, leave early or wait out peak hours to avoid surge pricing, walk a few blocks away from crowded areas for easier pickup, and compare prices across different rideshare apps.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County zoning board recommends denial of controversial data center near Arden
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Planning and Zoning Board unanimously voted Thursday to recommend denial of Project Tango, a proposed AI data center near Arden community and Saddle View Elementary School.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Planning and Zoning Board unanimously voted Thursday to recommend that county commissioners deny Project Tango, a proposed hyperscale AI data center planned near the Arden community and Saddle View Elementary School in western Palm Beach County. The recommendation followed a nearly five-hour public hearing at the Vista Center that drew more than 100 attendees, with more than 40 residents speaking during public comment. The proposed facility would be built approximately 1,100 feet from the Arden community and the recently opened Saddle View Elementary School.

One of the central issues during the hearing was how the project should be classified under the county's land development code. Board members questioned whether the proposed data center qualifies as light industrial or should instead be considered heavy industrial. Under county regulations, light industrial uses cannot create impacts beyond their property lines, and board members said they were not presented with enough evidence to conclude the facility would meet that standard. The project now heads to the Palm Beach County Commission, which will make the final decision during a July 15 public hearing. County commissioners will consider both the planning staff's recommendation for approval and the Planning and Zoning Board's recommendation for denial.

cards.headline: Lantana veteran gets lien removed, roof repaired after contractor dispute

cards.body:
Stephen McCoy, a disabled and retired veteran from Lantana, faced months of frustration after hiring Seabreeze Roofing and Sheet Metal in Boynton Beach to replace his nearly 20-year-old roof before hurricane season. He made six payments totaling more than $17,000 but said the company left two holes unfinished on the back of his home and stopped responding to his calls, texts and emails starting in January. After seeing no response from the contractor, McCoy came to WPTV's Let's Hear It event in Boynton Beach seeking help.

The situation worsened when letters from Gulfeagle Supply warned that a nearly $7,000 lien had been filed on his home because the supply company had furnished materials to Seabreeze Roofing for McCoy's property but was not paid. Within an hour of WPTV speaking with the Seabreeze Roofing owner, Gulfeagle Supply signed and notarized a final waiver of lien, lifting the lien from McCoy's home. About an hour after McCoy received the waiver, crews returned to his roof to finish the unfinished repairs.
